source: Mathesis (2025) Towards Formal Theorem Proving from Natural Languages (LeanScorer)
finding: Gap 1 and 2. Compares three reference-free semantic checkers against human labels on a subset of Gaokao-Formal, all run with DeepSeek-V3. Re-informalisation (formalise, translate back, compare) has high precision but misses half of the wrong statements. A plain LLM judge has perfect recall but many false positives. A staged scorer (LeanScorer) is best.
numbers: Precision / recall / F1: LLM-as-judge 73 / 100 / 0.85; re-informalisation 93 / 50 / 0.65; LeanScorer (threshold 0.6) 94 / 89 / 0.92. Autoformalizer LC+LSC@6 on Gaokao-Formal 71% vs Kimina 49%.
quote: While the LLM-as-a-Judge exhibits perfect recall, its lower precision indicates a higher rate of false positives.
limits: Size of the human-labelled subset not stated in the text I read. Self-reported by the system authors. Wrong statements were deliberately kept in the set. Single judge model.
agent_relevance: Round trip alone is a poor detector (recall 0.50). Use it as a cheap precision filter, not as the only gate. A staged semantic judge beats both.

source: Sun, Sheng, Padon, Barrett (2023) Clover: Closed-Loop Verifiable Code Generation
finding: Round-trip style consistency checking among code, docstring and formal annotations: reconstruct one component from another with GPT-4 and test equivalence. Six directed checks must all pass. Accepts most correct items and rejects every adversarial wrong one on a small hand-made set.
numbers: CloverBench: 60 textbook-level Dafny programs, 5 variants each (1 correct, 4 adversarial wrong). Accepts up to 87% of correct, rejects 100% of adversarial wrong (no false positives). On MBPP-DFY-50 accepts 89% of correct and flags 6 incorrect programs in the human-written set.
quote: consistency checker achieves a promising acceptance rate (up to 87%) for correct instances while maintaining zero tolerance for adversarial incorrect ones
limits: Small, textbook programs. Adversarial variants were written by the authors, so they may be easier than natural errors. Contamination discussed only in an appendix. Code and specs, not maths statements.
agent_relevance: Multi-edge consistency (docstring to spec to code and back) with a hard formal check on one edge gives a very low false-accept rate. Cost is lost recall (13% of correct rejected).

source: Amrollahi, Lopez, Barrett (2026) Faithful Autoformalization via Roundtrip Verification and Repair
finding: Formalise, translate back, re-formalise, then check equivalence with an SMT solver. Statements that fail the check show more natural-language-inference drift than those that pass. Diagnosis-guided scoped repair of the failing stage is the best repair method when the diagnoser is reliable. Validated against an NLI model, not against human labels.
numbers: 150 Texas Transportation Code rules and 77 Parks and Wildlife rules; Claude Opus 4.6 and GPT-5.2. Equivalence without repair 44.7% (Traffic, Claude) to 67.1% (Wildlife, GPT). Failing rules show 1.4 to 2.5 times more NLI drift than passing rules. With GPT as diagnoser scoped repair loses its lead; with Claude as diagnoser it regains it.
quote: rules that fail the equivalence check show 1.4-2.5 more natural language inference (NLI) drift than rules that pass it
limits: Statutory text, not maths. Ground truth is a BART-large NLI proxy, so this does not close gap 1 against human labels. Reconstructed text is wordier, which NLI reads as 'strengthened'. Authors do not claim results transfer to maths.
agent_relevance: Round trip is a usable signal where no reference exists, but only weakly validated. Repair should be localised to the stage the diagnoser blames, and the diagnoser must be a strong model.

source: Beyond Compilation (2026) Evaluating Faithful Natural-Language-to-Lean Statement Formalization
finding: Gap 2, 5, 8. Criterion = Lean compiles AND two LLM judges from different families agree. It matches the human majority on 91.5% of an independent audit, beating a LeanScorer-style rule. Compiling overstates faithfulness by 1.3 to 29.5 points across eight systems. For the two newest models most rejections are judge errors, not translation errors.
numbers: 227 university-level statements, 8 systems. Audit 54/59 = 91.5% (95% CI 81.6-96.3); positive precision 44/46 = 95.7%; negative confirmation 10/13 = 76.9%. Compile+LeanScorer rule: 45/59 (76.3%) agreement. Tool-augmented agent compiles 87.2% but 57.7% accepted; 23.8 of 29.5 gap points confirmed real by human review. One-shot gap shares 78-100% real errors for six systems. For the two newest models only 4 of 54 rejections (7%) are translation errors. Human held-out reviewer kappa vs other two 0.18-0.28.
quote: Lean certifies the theorem the model wrote, not that it wrote the theorem the user meant.
limits: Judges and reviewers are model versions named in the paper (GPT-5.2, Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6.1 Sol). Small audit (n=59). Authors note the criterion rarely accepts unfaithful output but rejects some faithful ones. Low human kappa shows the human label itself is noisy.
agent_relevance: Cross-family two-judge agreement plus compile is a strong gate. Best models err less than the judge, so a judge-only gate will wrongly reject their output. Add a stronger-model or human review step for rejections.

source: Dai et al. (2026) The Signal-Coverage Matrix: Stratifying Type and Semantic Errors in Statement Autoformalization
finding: Gap 3 and 5. At the same 4-LLM-call budget, three methods (Lean-Retry, Sample-Filter with N=4, typed-IR refinement SAF) tie. Their gains are about 64% type-stratum recovery; semantic errors stay about flat on net (14 of 16 rescued, 8 new created). Most Vanilla failures from a frontier model are type or elaboration failures, with semantic-only errors a small share.
numbers: DeepSeek V4-Pro on ProofNet# (n=186). Vanilla TS/SO/TO/BF = 95/16/61/14 (TC 59.7%, SF 51.1%). Lean-Retry 131/10/41/4 (TC 75.8, SF 70.4); Sample-Filter 131/11/37/7 (76.3, 70.4); SAF 129/11/39/7 (75.3, 69.4). Recovery of type-only errors is 23/61 for every method (Wilson CI 26.6-50.3). Two judges disagree by 26-37 points on elab-feedback outputs vs 7 on Vanilla. Opus+GTED precision 94.4-95.0%. Residual semantic errors are two gold-formalisation bugs.
quote: TC% gains should be credited by which cell moved, not by the scalar alone.
limits: One model on the fully dual-judged cell; other cells GTED only. Workshop paper. Equal LLM calls, not equal tokens. Semantic judge is another LLM.
agent_relevance: At matched calls, compile-feedback repair and sample-and-filter give the same result. Report which error cell moved. Do not credit compile-rate gains as faithfulness gains.

source: SHADOWBENCH (2026) Toward Reliable Automatic Evaluation of Semantic Alignment in Autoformalization
finding: Gap 2. SA-PASS gives full credit only if the statement compiles, implies each 'shadow' sub-statement, and is implied by their conjunction. It agrees with experts almost always and shows that compile rate hugely overstates success on research-level problems.
numbers: 178 postgraduate to research-level Lean 4 problems, 8 areas. Claude Code (Opus 4.8) with Numina-Lean-Agent: 61.8% compile, 11.2% SA-PASS. Binary agreement with expert judgments 98.8% over outputs from six agentic configurations.
limits: Needs hand-written shadows per problem, so cost moves to the benchmark builder. Expert label count not stated in the portion I read. An early version was used in ICML 2026 AI4Math Challenge Track 4.
agent_relevance: Decomposing the intended meaning into checkable sub-claims (forward and backward implication) is a strong faithfulness test. Our agent can draft 'shadows' as a self-check before formalising.

source: Zhang, Valentino, Meadows, Freitas (2025/2026) Beyond Gold Standards: Epistemic Ensemble of LLM Judges for Formal Mathematical Reasoning
finding: Gap 2. Fine-grained LLM judges (nine atomic properties, aggregated) rank formalisations about as well as a second human does, and a small model with fine-grained criteria beats a larger model with one coarse overall score. Humans themselves disagree a lot on exact rankings.
numbers: Two humans ranked 3 formalisations (human, GPT-4.1 zero-shot, Qwen2.5-7B few-shot) for 50 miniF2F and 50 ProofNet statements. Human-human exact match 38.00% and pairwise 70.00% (miniF2F); 22.00% and 68.67% (ProofNet). Atomic-property setting best in 12 of 20 exact-match cases and 17 of 20 pairwise cases. GPT-4.1 judged ground-truth correct 76.64% (miniF2F Isabelle), 82.79% (miniF2F Lean 4), 64.84% (ProofNet Lean 4).
limits: Ranking agreement, not binary faithfulness. Small human sample, one expert for the aspect analysis. LLM judges showed entangled aspect scores, humans did not. Table 2 text was garbled, so only headline counts are recorded.
agent_relevance: Score faithfulness on separate atomic aspects (logic preserved, objects right, no redundancy) instead of one gut score. The human agreement ceiling is itself low (about 69-70% pairwise).

source: Wu et al. (2025) StepFun-Formalizer: Knowledge-Reasoning Fusion (ThinkingF)
finding: Gap 5. Error analysis of about 10K outputs (GPT-4o classifier) plus a 100-example human subset split errors into natural-language misunderstanding vs informal-formal misalignment (wrong Lean object, logic structure such as iff vs one direction, type mismatch). Reasoning data written by a general reasoning model hurt, because it solved the problem instead of formalising it.
numbers: BEq@1: StepFun-Formalizer-32B 40.5% on FormalMATH-Lite and 26.7% on ProverBench. RL over 450 steps: reward 0.232 to 0.347 and average BEq@1 0.258 to 0.303. Figure 2 correct share (rows garbled in text): GPT-4o labels 33.7% vs 42.9%; human labels 35.7% vs 50.0% for Kimina vs StepFun.
quote: general reasoning model devotes its efforts to solving the informal problem instead of formalizing it
limits: Figure 2 and 7 percentages were read from garbled figure text; treat the exact split as approximate. BEq needs a human ground-truth formal statement. Authors' own model. Classifier is GPT-4o.
agent_relevance: Tell the formalising step not to solve. A reasoning scaffold must keep 'translate' and 'solve' as separate states, or reasoning will leak answers into the statement. Check the six listed error types explicitly.

source: Lou et al. (2026) Characterizing Paraphrase-Induced Failures in Lean 4 Autoformalization
finding: Gap 5. Rewording the same theorem with deterministic paraphrase rules makes frontier models output different Lean. Most of the inconsistency is at the code-generation layer, not semantic disagreement among outputs that compile.
numbers: Four frontier models (GPT-5.4, o3, o1, o4-mini) and three open autoformalizers. Surface consistency 19.1-49.5% (ProofNet#) and 44.5-55.5% (miniF2F). Compile rates in the set 6.8-24.2%. Hallucinated Mathlib identifiers are 34-50% of failures on ProofNet#; malformed syntax or elaboration failures are 47-70% on miniF2F. Among pairs where both compile, GTED median at least 0.943.
limits: Compile rates look low, possibly from strict whole-file settings. Preprint. Paraphrases are rule-based, not human rewordings.
agent_relevance: Wording sensitivity is real even for 2026 frontier models. Sample several paraphrases of the statement and compare, and give the agent library lookup to avoid invented identifiers.

source: Hu et al. (2025) miniCTX: Neural Theorem Proving with (Long-)Contexts
finding: Gap 4 (context). Giving the model the preceding file context (definitions, lemmas) more than doubles GPT-4o's proof rate, while the standard context-free benchmark miniF2F hides this ability. Retrieved cross-file premises help in a mixed way.
numbers: miniCTX theorems split 381 validation / 381 test. GPT-4o full proof average 11.72% without context vs 27.08% with file context (26.82% with context plus premises). Text states file-tuned model 35.94% vs state-tactic model 19.53% on miniCTX, but on miniF2F only 33.61% vs 32.79%. Time-split projects to limit contamination.
limits: Theorem proving, not statement formalisation. Retrieval used the LeanDojo retriever without Mathlib. Per-split mapping from garbled table is partial. Table row labels were garbled in extraction, so tuned-model figures follow the paper text, not the table.
agent_relevance: Supports the claim that surrounding definitions matter, as a second independent study beside RLM25. Keep file and definition context in the agent working set.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Improving Autoformalization Using Direct Dependency Retrieval (DDR)
finding: Gap 4. Models hallucinate formal dependencies (non-existent definitions or lemmas). Generating candidate dependencies directly and checking each against the library with a suffix-array check gives much higher retrieval precision and recall than prompt-based or embedding retrieval, and lifts autoformalization.
numbers: Retrieval precision and recall 0.8-0.9 for DDR vs 0.2-0.5 for prompted LLMs and embedding retrieval (R@5, R@10). Hallucination rate of ICL-retrieved dependencies about 0.22-0.36 per sample vs about 0 for DDR. 200 statements per difficulty bin. Autoformalization TypeC and BEq rise with DDR (e.g. Diff89 TypeC 0.385 to 0.770); exact column mapping from garbled table uncertain. Mathlib has over 240,000 entries.
limits: Fine-tuned on a 500K-sample dataset built by the authors. Test sets are small. Table columns garbled, so only ranges are recorded.
agent_relevance: Retrieve and verify names against the real library before use. A memory of past formalisations should store verified names, not free text.

source: Liu et al. (2023) LLM+P: Empowering LLMs with Optimal Planning Proficiency
finding: Gap 6 and 4. The LLM translates a planning problem to PDDL and a classical planner solves it. Direct planning by GPT-4 fails in most domains because it cannot track preconditions. LLM+P gets an optimal plan for the majority of problems, but only with an in-context example problem and PDDL pair, and with a human-written domain file.
numbers: 7 International Planning Competition domains, 20 tasks each; GPT-4 temperature 0. LLM-as-planner mostly 0% success in most domains; LLM+P solves the majority in several domains (for example about 90% in BLOCKSWORLD). Exact table rows garbled. Without the example PDDL context the LLM fails to produce correct problem files.
quote: Most failed cases are due to mis-specified problem files, such as missing one of the initial conditions
limits: Domain PDDL supplied by a human. 2023 GPT-4. Table I values not cleanly extracted.
agent_relevance: Formalise-then-solve wins where search or precondition tracking is the weak spot and a solver exists. A worked example in the prompt is required. Missing initial conditions are the common failure.

source: Chen et al. (2025/2026) A Reality Check of Language Models as Formalizers on Constraint Satisfaction Problems
finding: Gap 6. With modern reasoning models, writing a formal program for a solver is not better than just solving. Formalising underperforms solving in most model-dataset pairs and degrades with problem size like solving does. Reasoning models waste tokens solving inside the formalisation and sometimes hard-code the answer.
numbers: 4 benchmarks (NaturalPlan Calendar, Meeting, Trip; ZebraLogic), 6 LLMs, 2 targets (Python, SMT). Formalizer below solver in 12 of 16 reasoning-model/dataset pairs and 4 of 8 non-reasoning pairs; abstract says 15 of 24 (versions differ). Python beats SMT in 15 of 24 pairs. Weakest model (Qwen2.5) did better as formalizer than as solver.
quote: LLM-as-formalizer by no means trivializes the problem
limits: Abstract and body counts differ (15 of 24 vs 16 of 24). Workshop version. Constraint tasks only.
agent_relevance: Routing hint: formalise when the model is weak at solving or the problem is small and rigid. Do not assume formalising beats reasoning for strong reasoners. Forbid solving inside the formalising step.

source: Ye et al. (2026) VERINA: Benchmarking Verifiable Code Generation
finding: Gap 3, 4, 6. For code specs in Lean, spec writing is hard for frontier models and proving is harder. Verifier-feedback refinement beats independent resampling at matched query counts for proofs. Giving the true spec helps code writing, giving the true code does not help spec writing.
numbers: 189 Lean tasks. Best model o3: code 72.6%, spec soundness and completeness 52.3%, proof 4.9% (pass@1, ten LLMs). Iterative refinement lifts proof success up to 20.1% at 64 steps but at high cost; gains saturate on the hard subset (3.70% on VERINA-B). Run costs up to 1197 USD per model.
quote: iterative proof refinement reliably outperforms direct generation at matched query budgets
limits: Matched queries, not matched tokens. Proof task, not statement translation. Descriptions were manually enriched by the authors.
agent_relevance: Closest evidence for gap 3 outside maths statements: feedback repair beats resampling at the same number of calls, but gains stop on hard items.

source: Endres, Fakhoury, Chakraborty, Lahiri (2024) Can LLMs Transform NL Intent into Formal Method Postconditions? (nl2postcond)
finding: Gap 6. LLMs turn natural-language function descriptions into executable postconditions. Most are correct, and they can tell buggy from fixed code, so they are useful as specs. Postconditions caught real historical bugs.
numbers: GPT-4 test-set-correct postconditions @1/@5/@10 = 0.32/0.57/0.66 for one prompt and 0.39/0.66/0.75 for the other; compile 0.65/0.86/0.89 (@1/@5/@10, first prompt); 35 vs 47 bug-distinguishing items. 64 real bugs caught on Defects4J 2.0 (835 bugs).
limits: Correctness judged by tests on reference code, not by proof. Table rows read from garbled text so prompt labels are not certain. FSE 2024.
agent_relevance: Autoformalised specs work as cheap tests (bug-discriminating) on code tasks, a second place where formalise-then-check can help.

source: Ni et al. (2026) Draft-and-Prune: Improving the Reliability of Auto-formalization for Logical Reasoning
finding: Gap 3 and 6. Draft several natural-language plans, generate a solver program from each, prune executable but contradictory or ambiguous programs, and vote. Reported as better than the strongest AF baselines. Only the abstract was read.
numbers: AR-LSAT AF-only: 78.43% (GPT-4), 78.00% (GPT-4o); 100% on PrOntoQA and LogicalDeduction. Compared with MAD-LOGIC and CLOVER.
limits: Abstract only; token cost not checked. Logic puzzle benchmarks near ceiling.
agent_relevance: Diversity plus pruning of contradictory formalisations plus vote is a sampling-and-selection recipe for logic tasks.

source: Monotonic Reference-Free Refinement for Autoformalization (2026)
finding: Gap 2 and 3. Iterative refinement that accepts a change only if a composite of prover validity and LLM-judge scores does not drop. Only the abstract was read.
numbers: 100.00% formal validity and 90.27% overall score on miniF2F; 77.96% formal validity and 52.45% overall score on ProofNet (full-theorem setting).
limits: Abstract only. Overall score is the authors' judge-based composite, so it is not human faithfulness.
agent_relevance: An accept-only-if-not-worse rule is a cheap guard against repair loops that make statements worse.

source: TOMAP (2026) Efficient Test-Time Optimization for Multi-Agent Proof Autoformalization
finding: Gap 3. Instead of spreading test-time compute over all agents, find the bottleneck (the decomposer) and spend compute there. Only the abstract was read.
numbers: Improves over the best prior method by 19.0% on ProofFlowBench under syntactic plus semantic scoring, at lower test-time cost; most gains in a few iterations.
limits: Abstract only. Proof-level, not statement-level.
agent_relevance: Allocate repair budget to the stage that is the bottleneck, not evenly.

source: Miranda et al. (2025) Putnam-AXIOM: A Functional and Static Benchmark
finding: Gap 8 (indirect). On informal Putnam problems, accuracy drops sharply when the same problems are rewritten as fresh variants, a sign of memorisation. No equivalent test for autoformalization on fresh post-cutoff problems was found.
numbers: 522 original problems plus 100 functional variants. Best model 41.9% on originals and drops 19.6 points (46.8% relative) on variations; all 18 other models drop, 10 with non-overlapping 95% CIs.
limits: Informal answer accuracy, not autoformalization. Does not measure miniF2F contamination directly.
agent_relevance: Contamination is real for maths benchmarks. Test the agent on freshly made variants, not on miniF2F.

source: Tsoukalas et al. (2024) PutnamBench
finding: Gap 8. A benchmark of 1692 hand-built formalisations of 640 Putnam theorems (Lean 4, Isabelle, some Coq), built so that provers solve only a handful, unlike saturated miniF2F. Authors flag that GPT-4 informal proofs used in a sketch pipeline may be contaminated.
numbers: 640 theorems, 1692 formalisations. Provers solved only a handful at release.
quote: These approaches can only solve a handful of the PUTNAMBENCH problems
limits: Formal statements are human-written, so it tests proving, not translation. A fresh-problem autoformalization test is still missing.
agent_relevance: Use hard, human-formalised sets for proving and fresh problems for translation. miniF2F near 97% is not informative.

source: Yu et al. (2025) FormalMATH (annotation cost table re-read)
finding: Gap 9. The only cost figure found for human validation of autoformalised statements: 12 IMO-medalist-level annotators, 22 days, 6.89 USD per statement, after LLM filtering. Human stage kept 72.09% of statements; in total 21.7% of the starting problems ended as validated statements.
numbers: 5,560 statements; preservation rate 72.09%; 6.89 USD per statement; 22 days; 12 annotators; yield 30.1% to 21.7% after the last LLM check.
limits: No equal-faithfulness automated cost found. Cost is annotation only, not model calls. Faithfulness of the human-validated set not independently audited.
agent_relevance: No published matched cost for automated vs human. Keep gap 9 open; budget for one human check per statement at roughly this price.
